A different list with a similar start

scenarios.topic: Sieve compound tests and message size
scenarios.title: Combine review conditions with a message-size boundary
scenarios.summary: Combine project membership, review status and message size without moving unrelated mail.
scenarios.objective: File in Review only when X-Project exactly matches atlas and either X-Review exactly matches pending or the complete represented message is larger than 1024 bytes. Ignore ASCII letter case for these exact comparisons. Size includes headers, the blank separator and body, not just body length. Exactly 1024 bytes is not over 1024; pending project mail still qualifies at that boundary. Keep every nonqualifying sample in INBOX only. Run all samples and avoid extra mailbox copies. Equivalent supported conditions are accepted.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the failing sample’s Expected and Actual destinations. Distinguish a syntax or unsupported-feature error from a condition or rule-order mistake, then edit and run again.
steps: Understand the task
Edit and run the filter
Verify all sample outcomes

guide.title: Inspect two different reasons to review
guide.why: allof (test, test) means every enclosed test must be true. anyof (test, test) means at least one must be true. Separate tests with commas. Parentheses preserve the intended grouping: team membership AND (review needed OR large message).
guide.action: Fill worked example and select Run filter. Select Small orchard todo, then Large orchard ready. Read their headers, represented size and Actual results.

guide.title: Test the exact boundary
guide.why: size :over compares complete message bytes, including headers and the separating blank line. K means 1024 bytes, so size :over 1K means strictly larger than 1024. At exactly the threshold, neither :over nor :under matches.
guide.action: Select Ready orchard mail at 512 bytes. Change :over 512 to :over 511 in Filter and run again; restore 512 afterward.

guide.title: Compare anyof and allof
guide.why: A large message from another team must not pass a team-specific rule. Keep the team test outside the anyof group; otherwise size alone could admit unrelated mail. Missing headers do not match, but another true condition inside anyof can still make that group true.
guide.action: Replace the inner anyof with allof, then run. Compare the small todo and large ready cases. Restore the worked example and rerun.

scenarios.explanation: The outer allof requires the correct project. Its inner anyof permits pending review or a message over the strict size threshold. Exactly 1024 bytes cannot satisfy the size alternative, but can still qualify through pending status. Other projects remain in INBOX regardless of size.
hints: Read each failed sample’s project, review field and complete represented size. Separate the outer requirement from the inner alternatives.
The project condition must remain true even when a message is large.
At the size boundary, check whether pending status independently satisfies the alternatives. Do not change :over to an inclusive comparison.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded Sieve header/size/filing subset with plain represented ASCII headers and named virtual mailboxes. No real mail delivery, host files, shell, subprocess or network. LF script lines are accepted; message size counts canonical CRLF. No address/envelope parsing, redirect, reject, vacation, procmail, variables, MIME decoding or other extensions. Resource errors are explicit and never earn credit. See SIEVE_SUBSET.md.

scenarios.topic: Sieve rule order and safe recovery
scenarios.title: Recover an ordered filter without losing unmatched mail
scenarios.summary: Repair a filter whose overlapping rules create extra copies and override priority.
scenarios.objective: Urgent mail, identified by X-Priority exactly equal to urgent, must go to Review only, even when it also belongs to the staff list. Otherwise, mail with X-List exactly equal to staff-updates must go to News only. Keep all remaining mail in INBOX only. Ignore ASCII letter case and accept one matching duplicate field. Repair the supplied filter and run every sample. Preserve unmatched mail, respect priority and avoid duplicate destinations. Equivalent supported control flow is accepted.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the failing sample’s Expected and Actual destinations. Distinguish a syntax or unsupported-feature error from a condition or rule-order mistake, then edit and run again.
steps: Understand the task
Edit and run the filter
Verify all sample outcomes

guide.title: Diagnose the overlapping starter
guide.why: Separate if rules are independent. When both match, both bodies run; fileinto does not stop processing. A later keep also adds INBOX, even after another mailbox was chosen.
guide.action: Run the supplied example before filling it. Select Maintenance notice from the club, then Ordinary club update. Read Actual results.

guide.title: Compare a priority repair
guide.why: An if / elsif / else chain runs only the first matching branch. Alternatively, stop; ends the entire filter at that point. Use these tools to implement priority, rather than relying on the position of a filing action alone. The Stop button cancels the sample run; stop; inside a rule ends processing of that one message.
guide.action: Select Fill worked example, then Run filter. Inspect the same samples and Unmatched personal mail.

guide.title: Try an equivalent control flow
guide.why: stop without an earlier delivery action still permits implicit keep. discard cancels implicit keep and does not undo other actions, so it is not a repair for an unwanted extra copy. Leave unmatched mail with a deliberate keep or the default INBOX behavior.
guide.action: Replace the chain with two separate if rules, add stop; after each successful fileinto inside its block, and run.

scenarios.explanation: The starter runs independent rules and an unconditional keep, so overlapping mail acquires extra destinations. Prioritize urgent mail using an if/elsif chain, or stop after a matching filing action. Preserve the default delivery for everything unmatched.
hints: Start with the sample matching both urgent and staff-list conditions. Count its actual mailbox destinations.
fileinto does not stop the next independent if, and keep is an additional delivery action.
Either select exactly one branch or explicitly stop after a successful filing. Preserve INBOX for messages matching neither rule.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded Sieve header/size/filing subset with plain represented ASCII headers and named virtual mailboxes. No real mail delivery, host files, shell, subprocess or network. LF script lines are accepted; message size counts canonical CRLF. No address/envelope parsing, redirect, reject, vacation, procmail, variables, MIME decoding or other extensions. Resource errors are explicit and never earn credit. See SIEVE_SUBSET.md.

scenarios.title: File sender domains without matching display names
scenarios.summary: Classify mail by its parsed sender domain without moving look-alike addresses.
scenarios.objective: File in Partners only when an actual mailbox in From has the domain exactly partners.dispatch.test. Ignore ASCII letter case. Accept a matching mailbox in a list or any one matching duplicate From field. Keep every other sample in INBOX only. Display names, comments and Subject mentions do not supply a sender address. Longer or child domains do not equal the required domain; malformed or missing From does not match. Repair the supplied substring filter and run all samples. Avoid extra copies and preserve unmatched mail. Equivalent supported rules are accepted; this is classification, not sender authentication.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the failed sample’s actual mailbox address and field with Expected and Actual destinations. Separate raw mentions, selected address parts and full-address policy; edit and run again.
steps: Understand the task
Investigate and repair the filter
Verify every sample

guide.title: Run the separate domain example
guide.why: In Gardener <plants@orchard.guide.test>, Gardener is a display name and plants@orchard.guide.test is the mailbox address. The part before @ is the local part; the part after it is the domain. Names and parenthesized comments describe an address but are not the address.
guide.action: Select Fill worked example, then Run filter. In Sample message, compare Orchard sender with A display name pointing elsewhere and A different domain ending.

guide.title: Compare structured and raw text matching
guide.why: address :domain reads the domain from each actual mailbox in a named field. :is compares the entire selected domain. In contrast, header :contains searches the raw field text, including names and longer domains. The default comparison ignores ASCII letter case. Multiple mailboxes or duplicate fields match when any actual mailbox qualifies.
guide.action: In Filter, replace address :domain :is with header :contains, leaving the field and key unchanged. Run again and inspect the display-name and domain-ending samples.

guide.title: Check which field supplies the address
guide.why: orchard.guide.test differs from orchard.guide.test.elsewhere.test and team.orchard.guide.test. An exact test excludes both. Missing or malformed address fields do not match; spaces and comments around @ do not change the mailbox. Filing by a visible From field classifies mail; it does not authenticate its sender.
guide.action: Fill the worked example again. Change the quoted field From to To, run, and select The same address only in To. Restore From and rerun.

scenarios.explanation: The address test separates a mailbox from its display name and comments. Comparing :domain with :is excludes similar endings and child domains while permitting case differences and any matching actual mailbox. A raw header substring test cannot make those distinctions.
hints: Read the selected From field: identify the mailbox inside angle brackets, if present. Separate its domain from any quoted display name.
Compare the complete domain, not any occurrence of its letters in the field. A child domain is also different under this task’s exact policy.
Check the field being searched and remove unconditional deliveries that add another mailbox. Preserve INBOX when no actual From domain matches.
scenarios.simplifications: Address-enabled bounded Sieve subset with represented plain ASCII headers, dot-atom mailboxes, display names, lists and comments. scenarios.title: Inspect and repair an IMAP mailbox safely
scenarios.summary: Mark the support request as read, permanently remove only the expired probe, and preserve the unread report and the other account’s mail.
scenarios.objective: Use the supplied IMAP server; its configuration is read-only in this activity. For lee/INBOX: UID 101 (Support request) must remain and be Seen, without Deleted. For lee/INBOX: remove UID 107 (Expired test probe) permanently; a Deleted flag alone is insufficient. For lee/INBOX: UID 109 (Keep this report) must remain unread and unmarked for deletion. Preserve every other supplied message, including all of jo’s mail. Supported equivalent operations are accepted.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the failed outcome, compare the saved/running settings or actual message state, then change only the relevant configuration or protocol operation and retry.
steps: Understand the task
Investigate and change the virtual workspace
Verify current outcomes

guide.title: Connect and inspect safely
guide.why: EXAMINE INBOX selects the mailbox read-only. SELECT INBOX selects it for reading and writing. The reply reports EXISTS (message count), UIDVALIDITY (the mailbox’s UID identity) and UIDNEXT (the next unused UID). Sequence numbers count the current positions; UIDs identify existing messages even after positions change. A failed SELECT deselects the old mailbox.
guide.action: Choose imap-tls, Connect, then Insert and Send LOGIN for jules, EXAMINE INBOX and the PEEK command.

guide.title: Make precise changes
guide.why: FETCH 1:* (UID FLAGS BODY.PEEK[]) inspects every supplied message without setting its Seen flag. BODY[] normally marks the message read in a read/write selection. UID STORE 201 +FLAGS (\Seen) can also mark a supplied UID read. EXAMINE stays read-only, even when BODY[] is requested. A minus sign removes a flag; FLAGS without a sign replaces the supported flag set.
guide.action: SELECT INBOX for editing. Mark UID 201 Seen and UID 209 Deleted using the command picker; inspect FLAGS before EXPUNGE.

commands.explanation: Authenticate the worked account on the protected connection.
Select read-only before an exploratory fetch.
Inspect all three sample messages without setting Seen.
Switch to a read/write selection for the requested changes.
Add Seen only to the support request; UID identifies the message, not its current position.
Mark the expired probe; the stored copy remains until expunged.
Remove marked messages. Sequence positions close up, but remaining UIDs do not change.
Deliberately mark the report read to see a useful failure.
Remove only Seen from the report, preserving other supported flags.

guide.title: Verify and experiment
guide.why: UID STORE 209 +FLAGS (\Deleted) marks a message; EXPUNGE permanently removes all messages currently marked Deleted in the selected read/write mailbox. CLOSE also expunges in read/write mode, without individual EXPUNGE replies. EXAMINE followed by CLOSE does not expunge. LOGOUT, reconnecting and selecting another mailbox do not commit IMAP deletion flags automatically.
guide.action: Send EXPUNGE, then Check example. Try fetching UID 213 with BODY[] and check again; remove its Seen flag to repair that mistake.

scenarios.explanation: Inspect with EXAMINE and PEEK, switch to SELECT for edits, then target stable UIDs. Seen and Deleted are separate flags; only the required probe should be expunged. A read/write BODY[] fetch can also satisfy the support request’s Seen requirement.

UID STORE 201 +FLAGS (\Seen) can also mark a supplied UID read. EXAMINE stays read-only, even when BODY[] is requested. A minus sign removes a flag; FLAGS without a sign replaces the supported flag set.

CLOSE also expunges in read/write mode, without individual EXPUNGE replies. EXAMINE followed by CLOSE does not expunge. LOGOUT, reconnecting and selecting another mailbox do not commit IMAP deletion flags automatically.
scenarios.simplifications: Dovecot CE2.4.1-inspired explicit configuration profile and bounded IMAP4rev1/POP subset; no full daemon or protocol conformance. TLS uses supplied logical trust/name/day/key facts, not cryptography. Authentication and Maildir contents are supplied virtual fixtures. One client at a time, flat mailboxes, plain ASCII messages, Seen/Deleted only; no MIME, APPEND, SEARCH, concurrent delivery, external authentication, real network or host paths. X-SIMULATOR capability marks the partial IMAP profile. See MAILBOX_ACCESS_SUBSET.md for commands, limits and exclusions.

scenarios.summary: Restore secure POP access without breaking IMAP, then remove only the expired probe from the first account and preserve every other message.
scenarios.objective: Restore POP3 alongside the working IMAP service, using the existing protected per-user configuration. It does not delete the message.
guide.action: Fill worked configuration, save, restart and enable. Choose pop-tls, then Connect.

guide.title: Try a reversible removal
guide.why: DELE only marks. RSET clears all pending deletion marks; a disconnect or lost server session also leaves the stored messages intact. scenarios.title: Audit a pending change and clean up read notices
scenarios.summary: Audit a pending mail-path change, then preview and remove only read expired notices without touching protected mail.
scenarios.objective: Keep saved and running per-account mail locations consistent for both rowan and tess; keep the service running and enabled at boot. Keep both accounts' protected IMAP/POP access working and reject unprotected remote passwords. In rowan's INBOX and Archive, permanently remove every read message whose Subject contains [EXPIRED]. Keep unread [EXPIRED] notices unread and unmarked, preserve all other rowan messages, and preserve every tess message.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the failing outcome and actual command results. Correct the saved/running setting or refine the mailbox/user/query. If protected mail was removed, reset this attempt to restore its supplied messages before retrying.
steps: Understand the task
Investigate and change the supplied server
Verify current outcomes

guide.title: Inspect, repair and save the pending setting
guide.why: A running server can be healthy while its saved file would break the next restart. doveconf mail_path prints the saved setting; -h hides the setting name. It does not read unsaved editor text or apply changes. Here only named-setting queries are supported, not full/default dumps.
guide.action: Run doveconf -h mail_path before editing. Fill worked configuration, then Save configuration and run the query again. Restart service only after the saved value is correct; Enable at boot.

guide.title: Preview and apply the same precise query
guide.why: doveadm works on a server-side mail store. This workspace supplies that administrator role; it does not ask you to run sudo or contact a real server. mailbox list names a supplied user’s folders; search identifies matching messages by mailbox identity and UID. UIDs are not POP positions.
guide.action: Insert and Run command for mailbox list, then search and fetch for elin/INBOX with seen subject '[DRILL]'. Inspect the UID and Subject before running expunge with that same query. Repeat for Archive.

scenarios.title: Separate router administration from LAN transit
scenarios.summary: Separate traffic addressed to the router from traffic passing through it, then allow only the supplied administration, web and DNS uses.
scenarios.objective: Permit SSH TCP/22 to router 10.20.30.1 only from LAN 10.20.30.0/24 arriving on lan0. Permit traffic from LAN 10.20.30.0/24 arriving on lan0 and leaving on wan0 only to web server 203.0.113.9 TCP/443 or DNS server 203.0.113.53 UDP/53. Block other INPUT traffic to either supplied router address and all other FORWARD traffic. Preserve router-originated OUTPUT and IPv4 forwarding. Keep the supplied interface addresses and environment. Equivalent supported rule sets are accepted; do not rely only on the sample traffic rows.

guide.title: Inspect and predict
guide.why: INPUT handles traffic whose destination is this router. FORWARD handles traffic routed through it. OUTPUT handles traffic created by the router. An INPUT web rule cannot allow a LAN workstation to reach a remote web server.

guide.title: Repair the example

scenarios.summary: Match IPv6 control headers by direction, LAN prefix, type and code.
scenarios.objective: Permit incoming ICMPv6 type 2, code 0 through wan0 to lan0, destination LAN fd20:30:40::/64. Permit outgoing echo requests (type 128, code 0) from that LAN through lan0 to wan0. Permit incoming echo replies (type 129, code 0) toward that LAN through wan0 to lan0. These are stateless header matches. Drop other ICMPv6 headers, including wrong codes/directions, and all TCP/UDP for this control-only task. Keep supplied INPUT/OUTPUT, forwarding, interfaces and routes unchanged. A filter cannot route link-local addresses to another link.

guide.title: Inspect the actual IPv6 rules
guide.why: A packet header contains addresses and protocol information. ip6tables handles the supplied IPv6 headers; an IPv4 iptables permit does not apply to them. Read the rules from top to bottom: the first match decides, then the chain policy applies if none matched.

guide.title: Repair the separate example
guide.why: FORWARD handles traffic crossing the router. lan0 to wan0 leaves the LAN; wan0 to lan0 enters it. INPUT is for this router itself and stays supplied here. In the worked example, fd42:11:22::/64 is the LAN range. A /128 is one address, not the whole LAN.

guide.title: Test a missing code
guide.why: ICMPv6 uses a type and a code instead of TCP/UDP ports. Type 2/code 0 is Packet Too Big, type 128/code 0 an echo request, and type 129/code 0 an echo reply. --icmpv6-type 2/0 checks both numbers; --icmpv6-type 2 alone accepts every numeric code for that type.

After the experiment, remove the first inserted rule and retry. Inspect -S before deleting a row.

scenarios.explanation: The three separate permits describe different headers: incoming type 2/code 0, outgoing type 128/code 0, and incoming type 129/code 0. Replacing a type/code pair with a type-only match admits other codes; a single displayed host also fails a /64 requirement.

scenarios.objective: Save only these lookup meanings: report/tcp and reports/tcp select port 7443; report/udp and reports/udp select port 8853; clock/udp and time/udp select port 123. Comments, spacing, row order and canonical/alias choice may differ. Permit outgoing TCP/7443 and UDP/8853 from LAN fd66:70:80::/64 on lan0 toward 2001:db8:180::/64 through wan0 in NEW and ESTABLISHED contexts. Permit their reverse traffic only in ESTABLISHED context with the matching service source port. Replace the obsolete numeric permits: saving a mapping alone does not update installed rules. Block other TCP/UDP, including old ports, crossed protocol numbers, unsolicited arrivals and wrong ranges/directions. All addresses in the stated ranges must work, not only displayed samples. Keep incoming ICMPv6 type 2, code 0 from wan0 to that LAN through lan0; block other modeled ICMPv6 headers. Keep supplied INPUT/OUTPUT, forwarding, routes and interfaces unchanged. Use Check work after saving the file and repairing the current policy. Equivalent supported names, aliases, numeric ports and rule arrangements are accepted; editing either workspace invalidates old feedback.

guide.title: Repair the example mapping
guide.why: cat /etc/services shows the simulated saved file. getent services previews/tcp asks for the TCP meaning of that alias; /udp asks separately. A successful lookup proves a mapping exists, not that a server is running or traffic can pass. The supplied listener ports are the task facts.

Keep the supplied persistent addresses, routes and forwarding settings unchanged. Make both the running filter and saved /etc/lab-ipv6-filter.rules implement the complete policy. Save your intended editor draft; an unsaved draft or rules limited to the displayed clients is insufficient. Enable the provided lab-ipv6-filter.service and verify that a fresh startup loads the saved file successfully and satisfies the same traffic and full-range requirements.

scenarios.title: Repair client access using listener and scan evidence
scenarios.summary: Distinguish a filtered service from an absent listener, then repair the whole client-range policy.
scenarios.objective: On virtual server 198.51.100.20, keep TCP ports 22, 443 and 9000 reachable for the whole Admin range 10.20.0.0/24. For the whole Public range 10.30.0.0/24, keep 443 reachable but filter 22 and 9000. A single displayed client address is not the whole range. Keep diagnostic TCP 80 reachable enough to report closed from both observer positions; no service should be started there. Preserve all supplied processes and listener owners. Repair the current host filter, then Check configuration.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare ss with both observer views. A filtered connection is inconclusive about whether a listener exists; a blanket drop also breaks required access.

Compare the two observer positions

guide.title: Separate local listeners from client access
guide.why: ss describes supplied sockets; it does not establish whether a remote connection reaches them. The first INPUT decision may block a healthy listener.

guide.why: The example uses Admin 10.50.0.0/24 and Public 10.60.0.0/24. Correct the range decision; avoid a rule for only one displayed client.
guide.action: In Server terminal remove the wrong first rule with iptables -D INPUT 1. Add Public-range drops for TCP 22 and 9000. Repeat both scans and choose Check example. Then try the independent assignment.

scenarios.explanation: The server already has a valid SSH listener; the initial Admin failure is caused by its INPUT policy. Remove or override the wrong source-range decision, filter Public SSH and preview traffic, and preserve Admin access plus HTTPS from both ranges. The deliberately permitted diagnostic port80 has no listener and therefore reports closed. INPUT and OUTPUT both affect the result; successful displayed samples do not establish the policy for an entire /24. Equivalent supported rule arrangements and prefix partitions are accepted.
hints: A TCP 22 listener already exists. Compare its local socket evidence with the rule source and the selected observer.
The existing SSH drop applies to the wrong client range. Rule order and the entire source prefix matter.
Keep the unused 80 diagnostic conclusively closed while preserving the real Admin services. Denying everything cannot satisfy the useful-access requirements.
scenarios.simplifications: Only one supplied IPv4 server and two declared reachable observation paths. Numeric TCP connect observations use fixed simulated source port 40000 and the host INPUT/OUTPUT filter plus supplied process/listener metadata. No real Nmap, packets, discovery, DNS, version detection, vulnerability inference, queues, application health, IDS or host actions. Current rules resume as saved exercise state; server boot persistence is a separate topic.

scenarios.title: Retire an exposed listener without taking down the useful services
scenarios.summary: Correlate socket owners, retire only the wildcard preview and verify both client views.
scenarios.objective: Retire the owner of the unused wildcard TCP 9000 preview. A paused owner or a firewall-only concealment is insufficient. Preserve the loopback-only preview on TCP 9001 and every approved owner, including SSH and HTTPS. Keep SSH on TCP 22 reachable for Admin clients 10.20.0.0/24 and filtered for Public clients 10.30.0.0/24; HTTPS on 443 must work from both ranges. TCP 9000 must no longer be open from either observer; closed or filtered is acceptable after its actual owner has ended.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Use the socket bind address and owning process together. Blocking a port and ending its owner are different repairs.
steps: Correlate the two preview instances
Observe the current exposure

guide.title: Correlate the two preview instances
guide.why: A shared process name does not identify which bind is exposed. The existing listener lesson explains addresses and signal behavior.
guide.action: In Server terminal run ss -lntp and pgrep -x previewd. Identify the wildcard 9000 owner separately from the loopback 9001 owner.

guide.title: Observe the current exposure
guide.why: The selected observer sees a connection result, not a full application health or vulnerability report.
guide.action: In Observer terminal run nmap -n -Pn -sT -p 22,80,443,9000 192.0.2.10 from Admin, then select Public and run it again. Note that 9000 is open from both positions.

guide.title: Retire only the exposed instance
guide.why: Ending a process removes its supplied sockets; pausing or filtering it does not prove retirement.
guide.action: In the example only, run kill -TERM 110. Scan again from both observer positions, then Check example. Try STOP instead after a reset to see why it is insufficient.

scenarios.explanation: The wildcard preview owner is the retired component; the same-name loopback process must remain unchanged. Ending only the correct owner removes its retained listener. A filter alone may hide an open listener, while STOP leaves its socket present. Verify required SSH/HTTPS access from both client ranges as well as the preview being closed or filtered. Supported TERM, INT and KILL approaches are accepted when all required owners and policies remain correct.
hints: A process name can identify more than one instance. Match the wildcard 9000 listener to its owner.
ss -lntp identifies socket ownership; pgrep -x previewd alone does not distinguish the two instances.
A paused owner retains its listener. End only the intended owner, preserve the loopback instance, then check both observer views.

scenarios.title: Repair a VPN peer's endpoint and identity references
scenarios.summary: Compare outside endpoints and supplied identity facts, repair one peer, and preserve both LAN paths.
scenarios.objective: Restore the warehouse peer's outside endpoint and identity references using the supplied server and virtual file facts. Trust the training authority and use the warehouse certificate with its matching key. Preserve the assigned roles, explicit peer-name/purpose checks, reciprocal tunnel addresses and both full LAN route policies. Save, apply and verify the virtual profiles; do not disable verification or redirect unrelated traffic through the VPN.
steps: Separate outside and tunnel addresses
Match identity references
Save, apply and verify

guide.title: Separate outside and tunnel addresses
guide.why: An outside peer endpoint identifies the virtual transport destination; ifconfig names the inside endpoints.
guide.action: Read the supplied endpoints and both profile fragments.

guide.title: Match identity references
guide.why: Authority, certificate identity, key pair and peer-purpose requests are different facts.
guide.action: Use the supplied virtual file table to inspect the client references.

guide.title: Save, apply and verify
guide.why: An edited or saved profile has not necessarily become the applied configuration.
guide.action: Save the changed profile, Apply profiles, test both directions and Check configuration.

hints: Compare the client remote port with the supplied server port; compare outside addresses with outside addresses.
The CA must match the supplied training authority. The client certificate and key need the same provided key-pair ID.
Keep the explicit server-purpose and exact peer-name checks; disabling verification does not repair a wrong reference.
scenarios.explanation: An outside endpoint and port select the other supplied peer. Authority, own certificate/key and explicit expected identity checks serve different purposes. Once those metadata checks and the reciprocal tunnel addresses pass, both LAN route directions must still be correct.
scenarios.simplifications: Finite OpenVPN2.6-style editable profile subset with supplied identity/validity/key-pair facts and IPv4 UDP/TUN point-to-point routes. These fragments are not deployable profiles. No PEM/crypto/TLS handshake, certificate creation, actual interfaces, host files, routing, packets, daemon, DCO, multipoint/push/iroute, TCP transport or external connectivity is performed. Unknown directives fail. Conventional supplied LANs use /1–/30; general route destinations support /0–/32.

scenarios.title: Restore outward and return routes across a site-to-site VPN
scenarios.summary: Repair both profile fragments so every required host in two /20 LANs has an outward and return route.
scenarios.objective: Restore both directions between central LAN 172.20.16.0/20 and depot LAN 172.21.32.0/20. Cover every ordinary host in both LANs, including hosts beyond the first /24. Keep unrelated destinations outside the VPN. Preserve the supplied peer identities, authority, transport and reciprocal tunnel addresses. Save and apply the current profiles, investigate the modeled paths and check the complete configuration.
steps: Verify the peer prerequisites first
Read outward and return routes
Cover the whole range without redirecting unrelated traffic

guide.title: Verify the peer prerequisites first
guide.why: Correct peer settings do not automatically create every LAN route.
guide.action: Apply the supplied settings and inspect the actual prerequisite results.

guide.title: Read outward and return routes
guide.why: A request and its reply need the appropriate route on different peers.
guide.action: Compare each route network and mask with the opposite LAN.

guide.title: Cover the whole range without redirecting unrelated traffic
guide.why: A sample host can work even though most of its subnet has no return route.
guide.action: Test a host beyond the first /24, preserve the outside-path cases, then Check configuration.

hints: Apply first: if peer prerequisites pass, inspect the route covering the destination on the source side.
A request can leave correctly while the other peer has no route back to a source outside its first /24.
Use each entire opposite /20 LAN; a default route changes unrelated traffic and is not an acceptable shortcut.
scenarios.explanation: The peer prerequisites were already correct. The outward route must select the destination LAN, while the other peer needs a route back to the original source LAN. The full /20 includes several /24 blocks; exact interval comparison prevents a few working hosts or a broad default from standing in for the required policy.
scenarios.simplifications: Finite OpenVPN2.6-style editable profile subset with supplied identity/validity/key-pair facts and IPv4 UDP/TUN point-to-point routes. These fragments are not deployable profiles. No PEM/crypto/TLS handshake, certificate creation, actual interfaces, host files, routing, packets, daemon, DCO, multipoint/push/iroute, TCP transport or external connectivity is performed. Unknown directives fail. Conventional supplied LANs use /1–/30; general route destinations support /0–/32.

scenarios.title: Choose the vendor fix without losing site settings
scenarios.summary: Read supplied vendor/release facts, apply compatible local fixes, preserve site text and verify the actual installed outcome.
scenarios.objective: Apply the supplied fictional TRAINING advisories for Training Enterprise Linux release 8. Keep relay-agent installed at a compatible fixed build (1.0-4 or later in the supplied release-8 set). Preserve the original site text in /srv/relay/agent.conf. Keep relay-notes and its supplied file unchanged. Leave declared package requirements healthy. Keep the installed fixed agent’s ordinary file at /srv/relay/agent.txt identical to its installed archive record, including text and recorded attributes. Use only supplied local archives; an artifact for release 9 does not meet this incident, regardless of its version number.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the failing outcome. A higher package version for another system release is not the required fix. If dependencies refuse the update, inspect the incoming requires and installed provides, then plan the complete set. Preserve the site file and unrequested package; reset only this attempt if you need to restart.
steps: Understand the task
Apply a compatible package set
Verify installed data and retained settings

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Vendor target release and full package build both matter. Query headers before applying the local package set.
guide.action: Read the supplied advisory and archive origins. Insert a query, then Run command; use the read-only inspector to compare current site text.

commands.explanation: Read the installed version.

guide.title: Apply a compatible package set
guide.why: A completed transaction can still target the wrong system or omit a required dependency.
guide.action: Choose supplied local archives using the advisory and dependency data. Enter the update in the simulated command field and select Run command.

guide.title: Verify installed data and retained settings
guide.why: Package version, compatible target release, retained local configuration and healthy dependencies all contribute to completion.
guide.action: Choose Check work, read any failing outcome and investigate that package or file. Retry after a precise repair.

scenarios.explanation: Use the supplied target-system and full package-build facts; upstream version alone cannot establish patch status. The compatible update changes installed data and preserves config_noreplace site text while staging .rpmnew. Verify every requested package and dependency. No running-process, signature, exploit or real CVE result is inferred.
hints: Compare the target product/release first, then the whole fixed-in build. The other-system archive is deliberately unsuitable.
The configuration is intentional site data. Inspect its current text; replacing it with a vendor default would not satisfy preservation.
Choose the compatible release-8 fixed archive. A whole-package downgrade from the wrong-release build is outside this subset; reset only this attempt if needed.
scenarios.simplifications: Fictional immutable advisory/origin facts and script-free noarch regular-text RPM archives. Whole-database declared dependency checks; no real repository, signatures, scripts, crypto, CVE feeds, exploit, running process, service restart or host RPM execution. Config update behavior is limited to same path/flag/attributes; undeclared or colliding sidecars and other unsupported behavior refuse atomically.

rpm_packages_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on installed versus local RPM records, package version ordering and declared provides/requires. You will investigate fixed vendor facts, choose supplied archives and verify retained configuration. No host package manager or service is run.

concepts.title: Read the advisory before choosing a version
concepts.text: A security advisory identifies the affected product, release, package and the first vendor build containing a fix. A vendor can backport a security change into an older upstream version. Compare the full package version and release against the supplied advisory; do not assume the largest upstream number is the right package. These TRAINING notices and packages are fictional, not current real-world security advice.

concepts.title: Separate target release from package release
concepts.text: Training Enterprise Linux 8 is the target system release. In 1.0-4, 1.0 is the upstream version and 4 is the package release. The supplied origin table says which target system each archive belongs to. A 1.0-5 archive for system release 9 is not the stated release-8 fix.

concepts.title: Preserve deliberate site configuration
concepts.text: The current configuration contains site-specific settings. RPM marks it as %config(noreplace). When the archived default changes and local text differs from both defaults, this activity keeps the site file and stages the new default as .rpmnew. Inspect the site text before and after updating. A .rpmnew file is an incoming default to review, not proof that a running service has reloaded it.

concepts.title: Check the installed file as well as its version
concepts.text: A fixed version header does not repair damaged application files. Compare the actual ordinary file with the installed archive in the read-only inspector. Exact reinstall restores that archive’s ordinary payload; this activity preserves the intentional configuration text separately. This checks supplied file data, not a real executable or vulnerability.

concepts.title: Choose a useful alert source
concepts.text: Use the affected vendor’s advisory for product-specific fixed builds. CERT coordination notices can provide cross-vendor context and links to affected suppliers. A port scan alone does not establish a vulnerable or fixed version. This offline lab supplies fictional notices instead of subscribing to live feeds. Bugtraq is a historical alert-source name still listed in the current LPI objectives, not a promise of an active service.

concepts.title: Verify the whole requested outcome
concepts.text: Run the selected local update, inspect actual installed headers and retained file text, then Check example or Check work. Installed fixes, correct target release, healthy dependencies and retained site data are separate outcomes. Changing a package after a passing check makes the current result unchecked. Running queries or the separate example does not complete the assignment.

repair.explanation: Restore the retained handover package without changing the fixed application or its site settings.
